title: Computer Networks, Lecture 1: Classful IPv4 Addressing
subtitle: Classes, leading bits, first-octet ranges, reserved patterns, and practical network and host counts

questions.q: What fraction of the whole IPv4 address space belongs to Class C?
questions.e: Class C fixes 3 leading bits, so it holds \(2^{29}\) addresses out of \(2^{32}\), which is 1/8 (12.5%). 1/4 is Class B (2 fixed bits), 1/2 is Class A, and 1/16 is each of Class D and Class E.

questions.q: An IPv4 address in binary begins 1011 0000. To which class does it belong?
questions.e: The first bit is 1, so it is not Class A; the first two bits are 10, which is the Class B prefix. Class C would need the prefix 110 and Class D would need 1110. The prefixes never overlap, so the answer is unique.

questions.q: The first octet of an address is 200. Which class is it?
questions.e: Class C covers first octets 192 to 223, and 200 lies in that range. Class B stops at 191, so 200 is not Class B, and Class D starts at 224.

questions.q: How many networks can be formed in Class A in practice?
questions.e: Seven bits are free (the first bit is fixed at 0), giving \(2^7 = 128\) combinations, but network 0 (all zeros) and network 127 (loopback) are reserved, so \(128 - 2 = 126\). The value 128 forgets the removal, 256 ignores the fixed bit, and \(2^{24}\) is the host count scale.

questions.q: How many usable host addresses does one Class C network have?
questions.e: The host ID is 8 bits, giving 256 combinations, but the all-0 and all-1 host IDs cannot be assigned, so 254 remain. 256 forgets the removal, 255 removes only one, and \(2^{21}\) is the number of Class C networks, not hosts.

questions.q: The first octet of a Class B address ranges over only 64 values (128 to 191), yet Class B has \(2^{14}\) networks. What explains this?
o: The second octet is part of the Class B network ID and has 256 values for each first-octet value
Class B uses 14 bits of its host ID for networks
Some networks are reused across several first-octet values
questions.e: The Class B network ID is 16 bits (two octets). With 64 first-octet values and 256 second-octet values each, there are \(64 	imes 256 = 2^6 	imes 2^8 = 2^{14}\) networks. The range 128 to 191 holds just 64 values, not \(2^{14}\), and the host ID is not involved in counting networks.

questions.q: Which of these addresses is reserved for loopback testing and inter-process communication on the same machine?
questions.e: The 127.x.x.x block is reserved for self-connectivity, loopback testing and inter-process communication, so it can never be given to a computer. The other addresses belong to ordinary Class A, C and B ranges.

questions.q: What is the practical number of networks in Class B?
questions.e: Two of the 16 network bits are fixed to 10, leaving 14 free bits, so \(2^{14}\) networks. Nothing is subtracted because with the prefix 10 the network ID can never be all 0s or all 1s, which rules out \(2^{14}-2\). \(2^{16}\) is the theoretical count.

questions.q: Which of the following dotted decimal addresses is invalid?
questions.e: Each octet is 8 bits, so it can only be 0 to 255. The value 256 in the third octet of 10.0.256.1 is impossible. The others are well-formed addresses, even if some are not assignable to a computer.

questions.q: What fraction of the address space is Class D and Class E taken together?
questions.e: Each of D and E fixes 4 bits and holds \(2^{28}\) addresses, so together \(2^{29}\), which is \(2^{29}/2^{32} = 1/8\), or 12.5%. The value 1/16 is only one of them, and 1/4 is Class B.

questions.q: A student cancels 255 from the Class E first-octet range because it looks like all ones. Why is this wrong?
o: Class E has no network ID or host ID, so the all-0 and all-1 rules do not apply to it
255 is a valid Class D value
The all-ones rule applies only to the first octet, and 255 is the last
questions.e: The all-0 and all-1 rules are about the network ID and host ID. Class E has neither, so no value in 240 to 255 is cancelled by those rules. The other reasons are made up: 255 is not Class D, and the rule is not tied to the first octet alone.

questions.q: Which first-octet value is a usable Class A network?
questions.e: Usable Class A first octets are 1 to 126. The value 0 is an all-zero network ID, 127 is reserved for loopback, and 128 belongs to Class B.

questions.q: In Class B the number of networks is \(2^m\) and the number of usable hosts per network is \(2^n - 2\). What is the ratio \(m/n\)?
questions.e: Practical Class B has 14 free network bits, so \(m = 14\), and 16 host bits, so \(n = 16\). Thus \(m/n = 14/16 = 7/8\). Using the theoretical 16 for m would wrongly give 1.

questions.q: Suppose a Class B style address keeps the leading bits 10 but uses 20 bits for the network ID. How many usable hosts does each network have?
questions.e: The host ID is the remaining \(32 - 20 = 12\) bits, so \(2^{12} = 4096\) combinations, minus the all-0 and all-1 host IDs gives 4094. 4096 forgets the removal, \(2^{18}\) is the number of networks, and 1022 would correspond to 10 host bits.

questions.q: For what purpose are Class D addresses reserved?
questions.e: Class D (first octet 224 to 239) is used for multicasting; the meaning of multicasting is the subject of the next lecture. Research and future use is Class E, and loopback is the 127 block of Class A.

questions.q: Which of the following give the correct leading bits of the class?
questions.e: Class A starts with 0, Class B with 10 and Class E with 1111. Class C starts with 110, not 111; the pattern 111 is shared by Classes D and E before the fourth bit separates them.

questions.q: Which of these addresses cannot be assigned to a computer?
questions.e: 10.0.0.0 has an all-zero host ID, 10.255.255.255 has an all-one host ID, and 127.0.0.5 is in the loopback block. 10.0.0.1 is an ordinary valid Class A host address, since only the two extreme host patterns are removed.

questions.q: Which first-octet values belong to Class B?
questions.e: Class B spans 128 to 191, so 128, 191 and 150 are inside. 192 is the first Class C value.

questions.q: Which classes have no network ID and no host ID?
questions.e: Classes D and E use the whole address as a single unit (multicasting, and research or future use). Classes A and B are both split into a network ID and a host ID.

questions.q: Which statements about Class A are correct?
o: The usable first octets are 1 to 126
Seven bits of the network ID are free
The practical number of networks is \(2^8\)
questions.e: The first bit is fixed at 0, so 7 of the 8 network bits are free; with 0 and 127 removed, the usable first octets are 1 to 126; the host ID is 24 bits. The practical network count is \(2^7 - 2 = 126\), not \(2^8\), which is the theoretical figure.

questions.q: In which classes is the practical number of networks exactly \(2^{	ext{free network bits}}\), with nothing subtracted?
questions.e: With prefixes 10 and 110 the network ID can never be all 0s or all 1s, so nothing is cancelled and the counts are \(2^{14}\) and \(2^{21}\). In Class A the network 0 and the loopback network 127 are removed, giving \(2^7 - 2\).

questions.q: Which statements about the sizes of the classes are correct?
o: Class D and Class E have the same number of addresses
Class C has twice as many addresses as Class D
Class A has twice as many addresses as Class B
Class B has the same number of addresses as Class C
questions.e: Each class fixes one more bit than the previous (except D and E, which both fix 4), so sizes are \(2^{31}, 2^{30}, 2^{29}, 2^{28}, 2^{28}\). Hence D equals E, C is twice D, and A is twice B. B (\(2^{30}\)) is twice C (\(2^{29}\)), not equal to it.

questions.q: Which hexadecimal-to-decimal conversions of a single octet are correct?
questions.e: C2: \(12 	imes 16 + 2 = 194\). 2F: \(2 	imes 16 + 15 = 47\). B5: \(11 	imes 16 + 5 = 181\). FF is \(15 	imes 16 + 15 = 255\), not 256, since an octet never exceeds 255.

questions.q: Which first-octet values belong to Class C?
questions.e: Class C covers 192 to 223. The value 224 is the first Class D value.

questions.q: An address has first octet 150. Which statements are correct?
o: Each network of its class has \(2^{16}\) usable hosts
questions.e: 150 lies in 128 to 191, so Class B, which splits 16 and 16. The usable hosts per network are \(2^{16} - 2\), not \(2^{16}\), because the all-0 and all-1 host IDs are removed.

questions.q: Convert the hexadecimal octet D4 to decimal.
questions.e: D is 13, so \(13 	imes 16 + 4 = 208 + 4 = 212\). The common error is to multiply the right digit instead of the left by 16.

questions.q: How many usable host addresses does a network have if its host ID is 10 bits long? Assume the all-0 and all-1 host IDs are not assignable.
questions.e: There are \(2^{10} = 1024\) host combinations; removing the all-0 and all-1 ones leaves 1022. Giving 1024 forgets the reserved patterns.

questions.q: The practical number of Class C networks is \(2^x\). Find x.
questions.e: The network ID is 24 bits and 3 are fixed by the prefix 110, so 21 bits vary. Nothing is removed. Answering 24 is the theoretical figure.

questions.q: How many networks can Class A have in practice?
questions.e: \(2^7 = 128\) combinations of the free bits, minus the all-zero network and the loopback network 127, gives 126. The figure 128 forgets the two reserved networks.

questions.q: Convert the binary octet 11101110 to decimal.
questions.e: The two 0 bits have weights 16 and 1, total 17, so \(255 - 17 = 238\). Checking: \(128+64+32+8+4+2 = 238\).

questions.q: How many usable hosts can one Class B network have?
questions.e: The host ID is 16 bits, so \(2^{16} = 65536\) combinations, minus 2 reserved patterns gives 65534. The value 65536 forgets the subtraction.

questions.q: How many different values does the first octet take across Class D (224 to 239)?
questions.e: The values are 224 through 239 inclusive, and \(239 - 224 + 1 = 16\), which is also \(2^4\) because four bits of the first octet are free. Answering 15 forgets the +1.

questions.q: What percentage of all addresses do Class D and Class E hold together?
questions.e: Each holds 6.25%, so together 12.5%. Each class fixes 4 bits, so each is \(2^{28}/2^{32} = 1/16\).

questions.q: A Class B style address keeps the leading bits 10 but uses 20 bits for the network ID. The number of networks is \(2^x\). Find x.
questions.e: Of the 20 network bits, 2 are the fixed prefix 10, leaving 18 free bits, so \(2^{18}\) networks (nothing is cancelled because of the fixed prefix). Answering 20 forgets the fixed bits.

questions.q: Convert the binary octet 11111001 to decimal.
questions.e: The 0 bits have weights 4 and 2, total 6, so \(255 - 6 = 249\).
